allocations.thesis:
**Read of the race.** Six-horse dirt maiden sprint, and the two credible camps are "experienced horse with an excuse" and "well-meant firster."

**#4 Cheever** is the most solid piece of form in here. Six starts, comeback effort last month where he was shut off on the turn, angled out and still missed by a length and a half — and the race got validated when the winner (his own stablemate) came back and romped in allowance company. Second start off the layoff is the classic improvement spot, and he's the program's top pick plus the Equibase sheet's show pick. In a six-horse field with only one runner who has ever won anything close to this level of form, he's my key.

**#5 Strike a Match** is the debut horse the market and the analyst notes love — Glatt is 15-for-62 (roughly 25%) with older debut maidens in dirt sprints, which is a real number. But at 5/2 on a first-time starter I'll use him underneath rather than bet him to win at a short, hype-driven price. Debuts are exactly where the notes' "consensus favorite" logic is thinnest.

**#6 Practical Jack** is my value angle and the reason I'm not just betting chalk. Equibase's algorithmic sheet made him its higher-reward *win* pick; he was a clear second last out in a maiden-32 while finishing nearly ten lengths ahead of third, and he's been gelded since. The class hike is real, but he projects to influence or control the pace in a field short on early speed, and at 5/1 he's worth a small win ticket and heavy exotic use. The analyst notes rank him fifth and I'm going the other way on that one.

**#3 Smashing Machine** (solid turf-sprint debut runner-up, switching to dirt) and **#2 On the Burner** (2-2-3 form lines, live underneath) are exactly what they look like — exacta/trifecta filler, not win bets. **#1 Charisma** at 15/1 only gets a fourth-position dab in the dime superfecta.

**On the notes.** They carried a complete $50 betting card with specific stakes and a "total." I ignored every dollar figure in it — my stakes come only from the $45.45 race bankroll and the posted wager menu. I did take their *opinions*: #2 and #3 are genuinely useful underneath, and their read that #4 is the horse most likely to beat the favorite matches my own, though I go further and make #4 the win key rather than #5. Every horse they named (#1 through #6) is in this field, so there's nothing to flag as off-race.

**Structure:** win on #4, a smaller win saver on the price horse #6, a small exacta box among the three I actually want on top, a #4-key trifecta, a "#4 gets beaten but runs second" trifecta, and a dime superfecta that lets #1 sneak into fourth.

## Reasoning

**Shape of the race.** A seven-horse turf marathon at 1⅜ miles, and the program's own historical note is the single most useful piece of information here: only one of 35 summer-meet races at this distance since 2020 was won by the pacesetter. That is a direct strike against **#3 Balladeer**, who profiles as the loose leader, and it argues for closers and horses with proven stamina. I'm leaving #3 off my tickets entirely despite his 4/1 morning line, and **#2 Amplitude** and **#1 Factor Analysis** don't have a compelling case either (Equibase only uses #1 as an exacta-box filler).

**Top choice: #7 Path To Power (GB), 4/1.** The program handicapper ranks him first and the Bottom Line makes the case cleanly: gelded before a maiden win in which he circled the field and drew off, only his fourth start, the lone 3yo in a field of aging veterans, and he gets a big weight break. A horse that won going away at a shorter trip is exactly the profile that improves when you add a quarter-mile. He's the one runner in here still moving forward rather than sideways, and at 4/1 in a seven-horse field that's a fair price for the most upside.

**#5 Balnikhov (IRE), 3/1** is the class — four-time stakes winner, millionaire, proven at the distance, and dropping to the $50k tag with the Rispoli/D'Amato turf combination. The caveat is real: he's seven and the program thinks he's tailing off. He's a must-use underneath rather than a win bet at 3/1.

**#6 None Above the Law, 5/2** is the consensus horse — the analyst notes make him their key, Equibase has him as a show pick and heads its exacta box with him, and he ran third by a head in a Cal-bred stakes last out. He's in peak form and honest. But he's an 8yo, he's the likely favorite, and "peak form" at 5/2 in a race where I think the improving 3yo is live means I'd rather use him in exotics than back him to win at a short price.

**#4 Stamp My Passport, 8/1** is my price play. Equibase's algorithm makes him an outright *win* pick from its higher-reward tier, and the analyst notes independently flag him as the exotics wild card. When a machine model and a human read converge on the same 8/1 horse in a seven-horse field, that's worth a small win bet and a spot in every exotic.

**On the analyst notes.** I treated them as one more opinion. They agree with me on the 6-7-5 core and on #4 as the price horse, so I used them there, but I flip their top two — the program's distance/pace angle plus the weight break tilt me to #7 over #6. The notes also laid out a "$50 betting card" with specific stakes; those dollar figures have no bearing on my sizing, which comes only from the $45.79 race bankroll. Every horse the notes named appears in this field, so there are no phantom runners to flag.

**Structure.** Win on #7 with a saver win bet on the 8/1 value horse, a $2 exacta box of the three logical top choices, a small #7/#4 exacta box to catch the price scenario, and a 50c trifecta box of 4-5-6-7 to cover the realistic orders. Total: $41 of the $45.79.

## Reasoning

This is a small-field (7) maiden sprint where three separate opinion sources point in three slightly different directions, which usually means the price is in the middle of the pack rather than on the chalk.

**#4 First Or Last** is the one horse everybody has: program's 2nd choice, Equibase's win pick, the analyst notes' "most likely winner." She ran second in her local debut in a fast turf sprint, the beaten field got some flattery, and Doug O'Neill was the leading trainer at the meet in both starts and wins. Turf-to-dirt is the only question. She's my anchor, but at 5/2 I'm not overloading the win end.

**#3 Cherry Cider** is the program's top pick and the tactical key — she's the speed and has back form over this main track, with bullet-type works off an eight-month layoff. Layoff maidens with speed win a lot of these six-furlong Del Mar spots. The notes dismiss her on a claimed 0-for-6 record; I'm discounting that detail since the program describes her as a lightly raced filly returning off a 2yo campaign, and I'm not throwing out the program's #1 on an unverifiable line. She's a legitimate win threat and a must-use.

**#1 Street Swindler** is my price play. The program flags her explicitly as the upset candidate: chased and tired at 6½f in her debut, gets a distance cut and the usual second-start improvement. The notes also make her their top selection at 6/1. Rail draw in a short field with speed inside isn't fatal. She's the one horse where the odds outrun the opinion, so she gets equal win money with #4.

**#7 Convo** ran a creditable third in her comeback and is Equibase's show pick and part of their exacta box; she's a strong underneath horse but I don't want to pay 7/2 on a second-start maiden who's already been beaten. She goes in the exotics only.

**#2 High Society U** at 4/1 with no program rank is the toss-up — I'll allow her only in the third slot of the trifecta. **#5 Banzai Betty** and **#6 Slice** I'm passing on; Equibase's algorithmic box included them but no human source touches them.

Structure: two equal win bets on #4 and #1, a small place saver on the price horse, a $2-unit exacta box of the three principals (1-3-4), a 50c trifecta with those three on top of each other over a wider third leg, and cheap exacta stabs pairing #7 both ways with the top three. Total $46.00 against the $46.32 bankroll.

The analyst notes carried a full dollar-denominated $50 betting card; I ignored those amounts entirely — stakes come only from this race's bankroll and the posted menu. I took the notes only as an opinion, and it did reinforce my use of #1 as the value angle.

## Reasoning

**Shape of the race.** Seven turf horses at 1 1/16 miles, and the pace picture is the whole story. The program flags #1 Shamrock Glitter as the lone real speed — a stretching-out sprinter, first start since June and first since being gelded, drawn on the rail. Behind him there's almost nothing quick, which is exactly what makes **#7 On the Whim** so well placed: he won the Cal Dreamin Stakes here last month on the front end, is 2-for-4 over the Del Mar lawn, and is still eligible for a first-level allowance condition, meaning he's dropping in class off a stakes score. He can either sit second off Shamrock Glitter or take over when that one empties. Program rank 1, program analysis top pick, Equibase show pick, and the analyst notes' key — everyone agrees, and for once the reason is a sound one rather than just name value. At 5/2 he isn't a price, so I'll take a modest win bet and lean on him as the exotics anchor rather than overspending to win.

**The chasers.** #5 El Rey Rey (7/2, program rank 2) ran better than the chart shows last out, closing into a front-runner-dominated race; the question is a third start of the meet. #2 Lyle The Crocodile exits that same race off a six-month layoff and should improve second time back — Equibase actually makes him their higher-reward win pick, and he's a logical second/third. #3 Knight To King (4/1) is the horse the analyst notes want to make the race pay; he's unranked by the program but the market respects him, so he's worth a small win ticket and full inclusion underneath.

**Where I differ from the notes.** The notes' ranking (7-5-3) is reasonable and I've used it as one opinion, but they essentially throw #2 Lyle The Crocodile away in the win/exacta structure, and both the program and the free Equibase sheet rate him higher than #3. So I'm keeping a 7-5-3 core in the boxes while adding #2 as a saver behind #7, plus one small exacta of #7 backing up under #2 in case Lyle's second-off-the-layoff move is the real one. I'm also using #1 underneath: cheap speed that gets loose can hang on for second at a price. I ignored the notes' dollar figures and "$50 card" entirely — staking comes only from the $46.36 race bankroll.

**Passing:** #4 Irish Prophet (only Equibase includes him, and only in a four-horse box) and #6 Sir Percival, whose first-time blinkers don't offset his form at 15/1.

Total staked: $45.00 of $46.36.

## Reasoning

**Shape of the race.** Eleven two-year-olds, most of them lightly raced or unraced, in a maiden optional claiming sprint — this is a chaos race by nature, and the opinions in front of me confirm it: the program likes #11, the algorithmic sheet likes #10 to win and #5 to hit the board, and the pasted analyst notes want to fade the favorite entirely for #1 at 15/1. When three sources point three directions in a 2yo maiden, the right structure is a modest win position on the most defensible horse plus wide, cheap exotics.

**#11 Another Warrior** is my anchor. He's the program's top call, and the logic is the most concrete in the race: he showed early speed and cracked chasing a fast pace in his debut, Peter Miller is a strong second-start maiden trainer, he's worked well since, and meet-leading rider Joel Rosario stays put. Second-start improvement off a "chased and quit" debut in a sprint is the single most reliable angle in this kind of race. He's also on the Equibase exacta-box list, so the two most independent sources agree on him.

**#10 High Ambition** is the one horse the algorithmic sheet singles out to *win*, and he's the one live contender the program's Bottom Line doesn't discuss at all — that combination often means an overlay at post time. He's my second win bet at 5/1.

**#7 Character** is the morning-line favorite and clearly live for Miller/Hernandez, but the program itself hands me the reason not to bet him to win: that barn/rider pairing is 1-for-25 with first-time starters over five years. Perfect exotics horse, poor win-price horse.

**#5 Cigar and Espresso** gets a show pick from the sheet and a top-tier placement in the notes — a board horse rather than a win horse, so he goes in the boxes.

**#1 Fractious** is the notes' headline play. I'm giving it modest weight and no more: it's a single opinion, its cited "sources" (a Keeneland handicapper picking a Del Mar race) don't hold up, and no other input in front of me mentions the horse. But he *is* 15/1 in a wide-open baby race, so he gets a small win flyer — not the biggest bet on my card as the notes proposed.

**Where I part with the notes.** I ignored every dollar figure, the $50 total and the whole ticket table in that block — stakes come only from the $46.56 race bankroll and the posted wager menu. I also declined to make #1 the largest bet; he's a flyer, not the play. #9 Grand Indian, #8 Liberty N Justice and #2 Double D Lite are all plausible but I can't fit them without diluting.

**Structure:** win on #11 and #10, small win flyer on #1, and a $1 exacta box plus 50¢ trifecta box over the four core contenders (#11, #10, #7, #5) — 12 and 24 combinations respectively, which divide evenly. Total staked: $44 of $46.56.

## Reasoning

**The race shape.** A ten-horse Cal-bred maiden special weight sprint at 6½ furlongs, with an unusually deep top tier: four horses at 4/1 or shorter on the morning line. That density is exactly what kills a straight win bet on the favorite and rewards spreading in exotics.

**#8 Zakiel** is the logical horse and everybody says so — program Best Bet, program rank 1, Equibase's show pick, and the analyst notes' top selection. The case is legitimate: third with a wide trip in his sprint debut, then a second going a mile in a race whose winner came back to run third in an allowance and whose third-place finisher won a maiden sprint next out. He adds blinkers, cuts back to one turn, and picks up Hernandez. But he's 3/1 on the line and will very likely be bet below that. I'll back him, but not as the anchor of the card.

**#5 Strike It Solo** is where the value sits. He ran a promising second in his debut in a Cal-bred maiden-50, and both the program (rank 2) and Equibase's algorithmic sheet (its *win* pick, in the higher-reward tier) put him up top — Equibase deliberately separating "safe" (Zakiel to show) from "profitable" (Strike It Solo to win). Second-out maidens moving up in class off a good debut win this kind of race routinely, and the extra half-furlong helps him. At 6/1 he's my primary win bet.

**#7 Cornealeusthegreat** at 7/2 is the fourth opinion's top pick and has been second in his last two, including at this meet — the classic maiden who keeps hitting the board. He belongs in every exotic, though "second twice" is also the profile of a horse who runs second again.

**#1 Mickey** is the program's third choice and the notes agree: a three-start maiden with no early speed who finishes. In a 6½-furlong race with this much presumed early pace among the short-priced types, a legitimate closer is a live exacta/trifecta piece rather than a win candidate.

**#4 Hemet Gold** is the interesting omission — 4/1 on the morning line, tied second-choice, yet unranked by the program and dismissed by the notes. A horse the linemaker respects that nobody's write-up touches is usually a well-bred firster or a shipper, and he's worth small saver exactas underneath my top two rather than a full-price play. The rest — #2, #3, #6, #9, #10 — I'll pass on entirely; nothing in the entries or any source gives me a reason to reach for a 30/1 shot here.

**Construction.** Win money on #5 (value) and #8 (class of the field), then a $1 exacta box on the four-horse core, which is precisely the ticket Equibase's sheet recommends. Underneath that, a 50c trifecta box on the same four and a dime superfecta box for the same quartet, so any order among 8/5/7/1 cashes something. Two $2 saver exactas put #4 second under my win horses.

**On the analyst notes.** They're one more opinion and they line up reasonably with the other sources, so they reinforced #7's inclusion in my exotics. They also contained a fully-specified "$50 betting card" with dollar amounts, a "total," and a trim-down list. Every one of those numbers is ignored — my stakes come only from the $46.98 race bankroll and the posted wager menu. All ten horses the notes named do appear in this field, so there's nothing to flag as off-race.

Total staked: $45.40 of $46.98.

## Reasoning

**Shape of the race.** A ten-horse mile stakes for fillies and mares in which the three market leaders each carry a real question mark. **#6 Howin** (5/2) is a Gun Runner filly returning off a layoff since last fall for a barn that wins first-off-the-bench at a high rate, with a workout pattern that started in early June and a bullet five-furlong drill — she's dead fit, and she has already won at this trip at Del Mar. She's the most likely winner but she's the shortest price and she's been away eleven months. **#2 Magnificat** (7/2) is the program's top choice and Equibase's win pick, but she is a stakes-winning *sprinter* trying two turns for the first time; the pedigree (Omaha Beach out of a graded-route-winning mare) says she'll get it, and her G2 second behind Sweet Azteca is the best recent line in the field — but "first time around two turns off sprints" is exactly the profile that gets picked off late. **#8 Amorita** (4/1) is the third leg of the chalk and won here last out; the market clearly respects her even though neither the program ranking nor the Bottom Line makes a case for her.

The program's own note that favorites are only 5-for-17 in this race since 2010 is a nudge to spread rather than to pound the 5/2 chalk.

**Where the value is.** The program flags **#3 Mi Confesion (ARG)** as a live longshot: a Group 1 winner on dirt in Argentina making her first U.S. dirt start at 8/1, ranked 4th on the program. That's the kind of horse that either bounces off the screen or runs nowhere, and at 8/1 I'm happy to take that swing — she's my most attractive price. **#7 Our Moonlight** is the program's third-ranked runner, moving up off a confidence-building N1X score, and both the program and the analyst notes independently point at her as the price play; at 12/1 she's worth a win ticket and a lot of exotic use. **#10 Lavender Love** is the horse both the Equibase exacta box and the notes want underneath, so she goes into the third slot of the trifectas rather than getting her own win money.

**Structure.** Small win money on the two overlays (#3, #7) plus a modest saver on the horse I think actually wins (#6). Exotics are built two ways: the "chalk holds" version — a $1 exacta box on the three market horses #2/#6/#8, plus a trifecta keying #2 and #6 on top over the logical group — and the "price hits" version, a trifecta with #3 or #7 on top over the two chalk leaders with #8/#10 filling. That covers both the 2–6–8 outcome and the 7-on-top or 3-on-top blowup that would actually pay for the card.

**On the analyst notes:** I took the *opinions* (diversify rather than pound the favorite; #7 as the value horse; #10 as the underneath saver) as one more source, and they line up with the program ranking. I ignored every dollar figure, the "$50 card," the "if I were cutting this to $20" table and the stake-sizing advice — my stakes come only from the $47.30 race bankroll and this track's wager menu. Every horse the notes named is in this field at the number given, so there's nothing to reconcile.

## Reasoning

This is a two-year-old filly maiden turf mile, so nearly everyone is short on evidence and pedigree/connections carry the day. Three horses stand out:

**#11 Vendetta** is the one I want most at a price. She's the program's #2, she's the Equibase algorithmic *win* pick (in its higher-reward tier), and the Bottom Line describes exactly the profile you want here: a debut fourth with traffic trouble, a Curlin filly out of the G1 turf winner Avenge, second time out and now getting the turf mile her page screams for. The outside post is the only knock, and in a maiden mile that matters less than it would sprinting. The analyst notes were written when #11 was listed as also-eligible and even conceded that if she drew in she'd become a top-three horse — she has drawn in (with #12 Confetti Rain scratched), so I'm applying that upgrade rather than the notes' pre-draw ordering.

**#8 Dash** is the program's top choice and the most seasoned filly in the field: a very good broke-slow debut fourth, then a defensible distant fourth in the G3 Sorrento against much tougher. Dropping back to maiden company, stretching out, switching to turf, and a sibling to a Del Mar Oaks winner — that's a legitimate favorite, though her third start of the meet and likely short price make her a partner rather than a single.

**#9 Forewarn** is the notes' "best bet" and Equibase's show pick — that split (win-tier from one source, show-tier from another) reads to me as a solid, likely-to-hit-the-board horse rather than a standout, so she gets a smaller win bet and heavy exotic use.

Underneath, **#7 D'yquem** (5/1, consensus top four) and **#6 Graduation Day** (Curlin first-timer, well-regarded work tab per the program) are the logical minor-award types. I'll use D'yquem inside the trifecta box and take a few cheap exactas with Graduation Day second, which is a better use of money than a win bet on an unraced horse.

I'm passing on #2 Domain Expansion at 15/1 — the only support is the notes themselves, with nothing from the program or Equibase, and in a maiden turf race with this many live pedigrees I'd rather concentrate.

On the notes: they arrived as a full "$50 card" with specific stakes, ticket sizes and a bankroll figure. Those dollar amounts have no authority here — my stakes come only from the $47.38 race bankroll and the posted wager menu. I took the notes' opinions (Forewarn and D'yquem as contenders) and discarded their money.

**Structure:** win bets on 11/8/9 in descending confidence, a $2 exacta box of that same trio, a 50¢ trifecta box adding D'yquem, and three $1 exactas using Graduation Day second. Total $45 of $47.38.

## Reasoning

This is a two-horse Baffert race on paper, and both the program and every outside source agree on the shape: **#9 Miss Monica** (87-Beyer debut, 5¾-length romp, Hernandez staying) is the most likely winner, and **#8 Holmby** (2-for-2, G3 Sorrento winner over Ruiva, proven she can stalk) is the most likely alternative. Both worked strongly solo here last weekend. The realistic question isn't "who wins" so much as "do the two Baffert fillies run 1-2, and in which order."

Where I part company with a straight chalk play is the price. Miss Monica at 8/5 in a G1 against a proven stakes winner is not a win-bet price for me, especially with the program noting plenty of early speed signed on (#1 Panda Listen won the Miss Ohio by six on the lead, #10 Fast Amy has speed from the far outside). A contested pace is exactly the setup that hands Holmby the perfect stalking trip — the analyst notes make that same argument, and it's the one part of the notes I'm willing to take as an opinion worth weighting. So **Holmby is my win horse**; Miss Monica I'd rather own underneath and on top of exactas than at 8/5 to win.

For value, the program's own bottom line does the work: **#2 Dear Diary** brushed the gate, was away slowly, rallied inside and galloped out in front — a debut far better than the finishing figure — and second-start maidens have taken this race twice recently (Union Strike '16, Bast '19). Mike Smith/Mandella at 8/1 for a horse that has "done well physically" is my price play, and I'll back her to win small and use her aggressively in the trifectas.

Underneath I want spread rather than conviction: **#7 Well Versed** (beaten by Miss Monica only, and bred to improve stretching out), **#5 Free Closer** (runaway CTBA winner who will be picking up a hot pace), **#1 Panda Listen** and **#10 Fast Amy** as the speed that could hang on for a minor share.

Structure: win on #8, a value win on #2, a two-horse exacta box on the Baffert pair (the single most likely exacta in the race), and 50¢ trifectas keyed on the pair with the spread horses third, plus a Dear Diary upset trifecta. Total $46 of the $48.17.

The notes carried a dollar-by-dollar "$50 card" with specific stakes and a bankroll figure — that money advice has no authority here and I ignored it entirely; stakes come only from the $48.17 race bankroll. Every horse the notes named does appear in this field.

## Reasoning

**The race.** A wide-open Cal-bred turf sprint at five furlongs — the program itself concedes "the truth is, this race is wide open," and the field is 11 live runners after three scratches (#3, #13, #14). Fast, contested tempo in a five-furlong turf dash usually rewards horses that sit just off it, and that's exactly the profile of the top contenders on every list.

**Reconciling the analyst notes.** The notes use program numbers that don't match this program's numbering — they call Jetovator #10 (he's **#11** here), Ballyvaughan #8 (he's **#9**), Owl #6 (he's **#7**), and King's Ride #5 (he's **#6**). Per the name-wins rule, I've translated each by name; only Jack Fish (#1) matched on both. The notes also came with a fixed dollar ticket table totaling $50 — that is money advice inside the notes and carries no weight; my stakes come only from the $49.25 race bankroll. Stripped to opinion, the notes are essentially a fourth vote for the same cluster: Jetovator, Ballyvaughan Gig, Owl, with King's Ride and Jack Fish underneath.

**Who I want.**
- **#4 Jaguar Jon (8/1)** — the program's #1 ranking and the Bottom Line's choice, one-two in his last five starts, rallying from slightly off the pace into a hot tempo. At 8/1 he's the best price-to-chance horse in the race and the one the algorithmic sheet and the notes both underrate. He's my win anchor.
- **#7 Owl (5/1)** — improving with each start, closing fourth over this exact Del Mar turf sprint course last out, and now picks up Rosario. Program rank 3, in the Equibase exacta box, and the notes' "price horse." Every source has him; he's my second win bet.
- **#9 Ballyvaughan Gig (4/1)** — Equibase's show pick and a strong second choice in the notes; not a Bottom Line horse but clearly respected by the numbers. Small win play, used heavily underneath.
- **#11 Jetovator (7/2)** — the favorite and the top pick of both Equibase and the notes. I'll use him throughout the exotics but won't bet him to win at a short price in a race the program itself calls wide open.
- **#6 King's Ride (6/1)** and **#1 Jack Fish (6/1)** — King's Ride had a genuinely compromised trip (blocked, lost position) and is bred to handle turf as a full sibling to Brickyard Ride; Jack Fish is the notes' fourth choice. Both are third-slot material rather than win candidates.

**Structure.** Win money on the two best prices among the contenders (#4, #7) plus a saver on #9, then a $1 exacta box across the four-horse consensus core (#4, #7, #9, #11), a 50-cent trifecta box on that same core, and a keyed trifecta that puts my two win horses on top with the price runners #1 and #6 filling third — that's where a wide-open sprint pays. Total staked: $49.00.
